### 5.2.1 Genealogical and Epistemological Dimensions

The genealogy of legal liability for damages arising from defective products is rooted in the long history of the industrial revolution, an era when steam engines, motor vehicles, and subsequently pharmaceutical drugs flooded the mass market. From the mid-to-late twentieth century, civil law doctrines across major jurisdictions—most notably the United States through Section 402A of the *Restatement (Second) of Torts*—underwent a radical shift. This transitioned jurisprudence away from the principle of *caveat emptor* (let the buyer beware) toward the doctrine of strict liability, which eliminates the necessity of proving negligence. The epistemology underpinning this transformation is deceptively simple yet foundational: the manufacturer, who extracts commercial profits from circulating a commodity among the public, is the party best positioned and most economically rational to bear the risk of loss when that commodity proves harmful (Calo, 2014). However, upon entering the era of cognitive computing and persuasive software, this epistemological foundation trembles profoundly.
